read.sections.0.heading.source: A thing can connect several places
read.sections.0.heading.back: One thing can connect several places

read.sections.0.text.source:
Objects can connect distant societies through making, transport, exchange and use. Ceramics, or objects made of fired clay, are useful evidence. Fired clay survives well, and vessels were made in large numbers. Their histories connect artistic decisions with workshops, ships and people's demand for goods. Southeast Asian makers took an active part in these networks.

A Vietnamese dish in The Metropolitan Museum of Art shows a bird flying among clouds. It is dated to the early sixteenth century. The museum says it was probably made in Hai D'uong Province. This is an attribution, a reasoned identification of where it was made. The bird is painted in cobalt blue under a transparent glaze, a glass-like coating. The free brushwork shows a practised skill in decorating many vessels.

The dish was recovered from the cargo of the Hoi An shipwreck, near central Vietnam. The cargo was found in the late 1990s. It showed how large Vietnamese production of glazed ceramics had been.
read.sections.0.text.back:
Objects can connect distant societies through making, transport, exchange and use. Ceramics, or objects of fired clay, are useful evidence. Fired clay can last a long time, and vessels were made in large numbers. Their history connects artists' decisions with workshops, ships and people's demand for goods. Makers in Southeast Asia took an active part in these networks.

A dish from Vietnam in The Metropolitan Museum of Art shows a bird flying among clouds. The museum dates the dish to the early 16th century. The museum says this dish was probably made in Hai D'uong Province. This is an attribution, that is, a reasoned identification of where the object was made. The bird is painted in cobalt blue under a clear glaze, that is, a glass-like coating. Its free brushwork shows a practised skill in decorating many vessels.

The dish was raised from the cargo of the Hoi An shipwreck, near central Vietnam. The cargo was found in the late 1990s. The cargo showed how large the production of glazed ceramics in Vietnam had been.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Bengkel kerja" for "workshop" (glossary word), flagged: "sanggar" or "tempat kerja perajin" are possible. Keep "mungkin" (probably) in the attribution.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Objects can link places that are far apart. People make them, carry them, trade them and use them. Ceramics are things made of baked clay. They are good evidence. Baked clay lasts a long time. And people made very many of them. Makers in Southeast Asia played a big part in this trade.

A dish in a museum in New York shows a bird in clouds. It is from the early 1500s. The museum says it was probably made in Hai D'uong, in Vietnam. This is an attribution. It is a careful, reasoned idea of where it was made. The bird is painted in blue under a clear glaze. A glaze is a shiny coat, like glass. The quick brush lines show a skilled hand.

The dish was in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. Cargo means goods carried together. The wreck was found in the late 1990s. It showed that Vietnam made a huge number of glazed dishes.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Objects can connect places that are far apart. People make them, carry them, trade them and use them. Ceramics are things made of fired clay. Ceramics are good evidence. Fired clay lasts long. And people made very many of them. Makers in Southeast Asia played a big part in this trade.

A dish in a museum in New York shows a bird among clouds. The dish is from the early 1500s. The museum says the dish was probably made in Hai D'uong, in Vietnam. This is an attribution. An attribution is a careful, reasoned guess about where an object was made. The bird is painted in blue under a clear glaze. A glaze is a shiny coat, like glass. The quick brush lines show a skilled hand.

The dish was in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. Cargo means goods carried together. The shipwreck was found in the late 1990s. The ship showed that Vietnam made very many glazed dishes.

read.sections.1.text.source:
The dish was part of a regional economy. The Met records fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Vietnamese ceramics made for use at home and for export. Indonesia was a market for Chinese and Southeast Asian wares. Vietnamese makers produced vessels shaped like animals as well as dishes. They also made tiles used on Indonesian mosques and other buildings. Exchange connected objects for the home, decoration on buildings and religious settings. But this pattern does not tell us who bought the pictured dish, or where it was going.

Making ceramics also had a local history. Under the early Lê dynasty, in the fifteenth century, policies encouraged industry and trade. Specialised craft communities supplied different customers. The Vietnam National Museum of History names Bát Tràng, near Hanoi, and Nam Sách in Hải Dương as important centres for blue-and-white ceramics. Makers there supplied everyday vessels and special forms for buyers at home and overseas. So Vietnam was a place where people organised production and made choices. It was not just a stopping point between other societies. Still, this does not prove which kiln, or pottery oven, made this dish.

The dish's materials explain part of how it looks. Cobalt gives the blue decoration, and the clear glaze lets the brushwork show. People in a workshop worked together on shaping, decorating and firing. Making many vessels did not make each person's skill disappear. A workshop joined learned artistic knowledge to the practical work of supplying goods.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The dish was part of a regional economy. The Met records Vietnamese ceramics of the 15th and 16th centuries made for use at home and for export. Indonesia was a market for goods from China and Southeast Asia. Vietnamese makers made vessels shaped like animals as well as dishes. They also made tiles used on mosques and other buildings in Indonesia. Exchange connected objects for the home, decoration on buildings and religious places. But this pattern does not tell us who bought the dish in this picture, or where it was going to be taken.

Making ceramics also had a local history. Under the early Lê dynasty, in the 15th century, policies encouraged industry and trade. Specialised craft communities supplied different customers. The Vietnam National Museum of History names Bát Tràng, near Hanoi, and Nam Sách in Hải Dương as important centres of blue-and-white ceramics. Makers there supplied everyday vessels and special forms for buyers at home and abroad. So Vietnam was a place where people organised production and made choices. Vietnam was not just a stopping place between other societies. Even so, this does not prove which kiln, or pottery-firing place, made this dish.

The dish's materials explain part of how it looks. Cobalt gives the blue colour of its decoration, and the clear glaze makes its brushwork visible. People in a workshop worked together on shaping, decorating and firing. Making many vessels did not make each person's skill disappear. A workshop joined learned artistic knowledge with the practical work of supplying goods.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Kiln" is "tungku", explained once as a place for firing pottery.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Vietnam was part of a big trade area. The Met says Vietnamese makers made pots for home and to sell abroad. Indonesia bought pots from China and Southeast Asia. Vietnamese makers also made pots shaped like animals. They made tiles for mosques and other buildings in Indonesia. But we do not know who bought this dish. We do not know where it was going.

In the 1400s, the Lê rulers of Vietnam helped craft and trade grow. Some places were known for blue-and-white pots. A museum in Hanoi names two: Bát Tràng and Nam Sách. They made pots for people at home and far away. So Vietnamese people planned and chose their own work. Vietnam was not just a stop between other places. But we do not know which oven baked this dish.

The blue paint came from cobalt. The clear glaze lets the brush lines show. In a workshop, people shaped, painted and baked the pots together. They made many pots. But each maker still needed skill.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Vietnam was part of a big trade area. According to The Met, Vietnamese makers made vessels for use in their own country. They also made vessels to sell abroad. Indonesia bought vessels from China and Southeast Asia. Vietnamese makers also made vessels shaped like animals. They made tiles for mosques and other buildings in Indonesia. But we do not know who bought this dish. We do not know where the dish was going to be taken.

In the 1400s, the Lê rulers of Vietnam helped craft and trade grow. Some places were famous for blue-and-white ceramics. A museum in Hanoi names two places: Bát Tràng and Nam Sách. Those places made vessels for people at home and far away. So Vietnamese people planned and chose their own work. Vietnam was not just a stopping place between other places. But we do not know which kiln fired this dish.

The blue paint came from cobalt. The clear glaze makes the brush lines visible. In a workshop, people shaped, painted and fired vessels together. They made many vessels. But each maker still needed skill.

read.sections.2.text.source:
A seventeenth-century bronze covered box made in China shows a different connection. Its lid carries an Arabic religious inscription, writing that calls on God's mercy and compassion. The museum places it in the Kangxi period of the Qing dynasty. Chinese making and Arabic religious expression show why a label naming one place cannot describe every relationship in an object. An inscription can be writing and a designed part of a surface at the same time. It does not tell us who used this box, or prove that it was sent abroad.

Exchange was more than goods moving between points on a map. Makers served different uses and audiences. Objects carried designs and religious expressions as well as materials. Particular works reveal these relationships, while parts of their journeys stay uncertain.
read.sections.2.text.back:
A 17th-century bronze box with a lid made in China shows a different connection. Its lid carries an Arabic religious inscription, writing that asks for God's mercy and compassion. The museum places it in the Kangxi period of the Qing dynasty. Making in China and religious expression in Arabic show why a label naming one place cannot describe every connection in an object. An inscription can be writing and at the same time a designed part of a surface. The inscription does not tell us who used this box, or prove that the box was sent abroad.

Exchange is more than goods moving between points on a map. Makers served various uses and audiences. Objects carried designs and religious expressions, not only materials. Particular works reveal these connections, while parts of their journeys remain uncertain.
read.sections.2.text.note: "God" is "Tuhan", keeping the museum's own wording; reviewers may prefer "Allah". Don't translate the inscription further (educator note).

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
A bronze box from China is from the 1600s. It shows a different link. Its lid has writing in Arabic. This writing is an inscription. It asks for God's mercy and kindness. The museum says it was made under the Qing rulers of China. So a box made in China carries Arabic religious words. One place name cannot tell the whole story of an object. The writing is also part of the design. But it does not tell us who used the box. It does not prove the box went abroad.

Trade was more than goods moving on a map. Objects carried designs and beliefs too. They show us links between people. But parts of their journeys stay unknown.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
A bronze box from China is from the 1600s. The box shows a different connection. Its lid has writing in Arabic. This writing is an inscription. The writing asks for God's mercy and compassion. The museum says the box was made in the time of the Qing rulers of China. So a box made in China carries religious words in Arabic. One place name cannot tell the whole story of an object. The writing is also part of its decoration. But the writing does not tell us who used the box. The writing does not prove that the box was taken abroad.

Trade is more than goods moving on a map. Objects also carry designs and beliefs. Objects show connections between people. But part of their journey stays unknown.

write.example.source: The dish shows a connection because it was found in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. This tells us that Vietnamese makers made many glazed dishes that travelled by sea, and that they were part of a big trade in Southeast Asia. Its record does not tell us who was going to buy it or where the ship was going. We also do not know which kiln made it.
write.example.back: The dish shows a connection because the dish was found in the cargo of a ship that sank near Hoi An. This tells us that Vietnamese makers made many glazed dishes that were carried by sea, and that they were part of a big trade in Southeast Asia. Its record does not tell us who was going to buy it or where the ship was going. We also do not know which kiln made it.

Don't treat every shared colour or motif as proof of direct borrowing, and don't translate the inscription beyond the museum's account (a call on God's mercy and compassion).
